title: Network+ V9 (N10-009) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public N10-009 exam objectives. Not real exam questions.

q.q: A switch receives traffic on one port and sends it out only the port where the destination's MAC address was learned. At which OSI layer is that forwarding decision made, and what is the unit of data called there?
o: Layer 1, bits
Layer 1 only moves signals. A hub works there and repeats everything out every port; it can't pick one port.
Layer 4, a segment
Segments and port numbers belong to the transport layer. Switching doesn't use them.
Layer 2, a frame
Right. A switch reads the destination MAC address in the frame header and checks its MAC address table. MAC addresses live at the data link layer.
Layer 3, a packet
Layer 3 decisions use IP addresses, which is what a router does. A plain switch doesn't look at IP to forward.

q.q: A packet capture between a client and a file server shows many retransmissions, duplicate acknowledgments and the receive window shrinking to zero. Which OSI layer is handling these behaviors?
o: Network
The network layer handles IP addressing and routing between networks. It doesn't track acknowledgments or windows.
Session
The session layer sets up and tears down conversations between applications. Reliable delivery isn't its job.
Transport
Right. Retransmissions, acknowledgments and window sizes are TCP features, and TCP is a Layer 4 (transport) protocol.
Data link
Layer 2 can detect a damaged frame with the FCS, but it doesn't retransmit data or manage a receive window.

q.q: A user's PC shows "network cable unplugged." The patch cable is seated and the switch port shows no link light. Following a bottom-up approach, which layer should the technician focus on first?
o: Physical
Right. No link light means no signal on the wire. Start at Layer 1: cable, jack, patch panel, NIC and switch port.
Data link
Layer 2 problems (VLANs, MAC learning) only show up once there is a link. With no link light you haven't reached Layer 2 yet.
Network
IP settings don't matter until the link is up. Checking the address now would skip the layers below it.
Application
A bottom-up approach starts at the bottom. The application can't work at all without a physical link.

q.q: A sector's web app runs on four identical servers. The team wants requests spread across all four and any server that fails a health check taken out of rotation automatically. What should they deploy in front of the servers?
o: An intrusion detection system
An IDS watches a copy of traffic and raises alerts. It doesn't decide which server gets each request.
A load balancer
Right. Load balancers spread connections across a pool of servers and use health checks to stop sending traffic to a failed one.
A Layer 2 switch
A switch delivers frames by MAC address. It has no idea whether a web server is healthy and can't spread requests.
A VPN concentrator
A VPN concentrator terminates many remote-access tunnels. It isn't built to share web traffic between servers.

q.q: Security wants a device that sits in the traffic path and drops packets that match an attack signature before they reach the database server. Which device fits?
o: An IPS placed inline
Right. An intrusion prevention system sits inline, so it can block or drop matching traffic, not just report it.
A wireless LAN controller
A WLC manages access points. It doesn't inspect wired database traffic for attacks.
An IDS connected to a SPAN port
An IDS on a mirror port only sees a copy of the traffic. It can alert, but the original packets still reach the server.
A network-attached storage device
A NAS shares files over the network. It has no part in filtering traffic.

q.q: A unit wants staff web browsing to go through one device that caches common pages, filters blocked categories and logs the sites users visit. Which appliance does this?
o: A reverse proxy
A reverse proxy sits in front of your own servers and handles requests coming in from outside. It doesn't control staff browsing.
A storage area network
A SAN gives servers block-level access to storage. It doesn't touch web traffic.
A forward proxy
Right. A forward proxy acts for internal clients going out to the internet, so it can cache, filter and log their requests.
A load balancer
A load balancer spreads incoming requests across servers. Filtering user browsing isn't its role.

q.q: VMs in a cloud private subnet must download OS patches from the internet, but nothing on the internet may open a connection to them. What should the subnet's default route point to?
o: A VPC peering connection
Peering joins two virtual networks privately. It doesn't give a path to the internet.
A NAT gateway
Right. A NAT gateway lets private instances start outbound connections while blocking any connection started from the internet.
An internet gateway, with a public IP on every VM
That makes every VM reachable from the internet, which breaks the rule.
A dedicated private circuit to the data center
A direct connection reaches your on-premises network, not the internet.

q.q: A district office needs a link to its cloud provider that doesn't cross the public internet and has steady, predictable latency for a large database sync. Which option fits best?
o: VPC peering between two cloud networks
Peering connects networks that are both inside the cloud. It doesn't reach the office.
A site-to-site IPsec VPN over broadband
The VPN is encrypted, but it still rides the public internet, so latency changes with internet conditions.
A dedicated private circuit (Direct Connect / ExpressRoute)
Right. A dedicated circuit to the provider avoids the internet entirely, so latency and bandwidth are steady.
A client-to-site VPN on the database server
Remote-access VPNs are meant for single users, and they still cross the internet.

q.q: An admin must allow HTTPS in to a group of cloud web servers and block everything else. The rule has to apply to the instances themselves and track return traffic automatically. Which cloud feature fits?
o: A route table
Route tables decide where traffic goes next. They don't allow or block ports.
Network function virtualization
NFV runs network functions such as firewalls as software. It's a delivery model, not the rule set that permits HTTPS.
An internet gateway
An internet gateway gives a network a path to the internet. It doesn't filter traffic by port.
A network security group
Right. Security groups are stateful and apply to instances or their network interfaces, so return traffic is allowed automatically.

q.q: A new rule set must allow encrypted remote command-line management of switches and block the older clear-text method. Which ports are allowed and blocked?
o: Allow TCP 3389, block TCP 22
3389 is RDP for Windows desktops, and blocking 22 would block SSH, the secure option.
Allow TCP 22, block TCP 23
Right. SSH uses TCP 22 and encrypts the session. Telnet uses TCP 23 and sends everything, passwords included, in clear text.
Allow TCP 23, block TCP 22
That's backwards. It would allow Telnet and block SSH.
Allow TCP 443, block TCP 80
Those are HTTPS and HTTP, used for web interfaces, not command-line sessions.

q.q: Every router and switch must send its log messages to a central collector using the traditional, unencrypted method. Which port must be open toward the collector?
o: UDP 123
UDP 123 is NTP, for time sync.
UDP 161
UDP 161 is where SNMP agents listen for polling requests. It isn't used for log forwarding.
TCP 389
TCP 389 is LDAP, for directory lookups.
UDP 514
Right. Traditional syslog sends messages over UDP 514.

q.q: A monitoring server polls switches for interface counters, and the switches also send unsolicited alerts when a link goes down. Which ports carry each?
o: Both on UDP 161
Traps go to the manager's port 162, not 161.
Polling to UDP 162 on the switches, alerts to UDP 161 on the server
The ports are swapped. Agents listen on 161, and the manager receives traps on 162.
Polling to UDP 161 on the switches, alerts to UDP 162 on the server
Right. SNMP agents answer polls on UDP 161. Traps and informs go to the manager on UDP 162.
Polling to TCP 22, alerts to UDP 514
That's SSH and syslog. SSH could pull counters by CLI, but this question describes SNMP polling and traps.

q.q: A training video is sent once from a server, and only the workstations that joined the group receive it. Other hosts on the same subnets never see the stream. Which traffic type is this?
o: Anycast
Anycast delivers to the nearest one of several hosts sharing an address, not to a group of receivers.
Multicast
Right. Multicast sends one stream to a group address, and only hosts that joined the group receive it.
Broadcast
A broadcast reaches every host in the subnet, whether it wants the data or not.
Unicast
Unicast is one sender to one receiver, so the server would have to send a separate copy to each workstation.

q.q: A DNS provider announces the same IP address from data centers on three continents, and each client is routed to the closest one. Which traffic type is this?
o: Multicast
Multicast sends one copy to every member of a group. Here each client reaches just one server.
Anycast
Right. With anycast, many servers share one address and routing sends each client to the nearest one.
Broadcast
Broadcasts stay inside one local subnet and can't cross continents.
Unicast to a load balancer
That would be one address in one place. The key here is the same address advertised from many places.

q.q: Which port does a client use for LDAP directory queries encrypted with TLS from the start of the connection?
o: TCP 389
389 is plain LDAP. It can be upgraded with StartTLS, but it doesn't start out encrypted.
TCP 445
445 is SMB file sharing.
TCP 1433
1433 is Microsoft SQL Server.
TCP 636
Right. LDAPS uses TCP 636, so the connection is encrypted from the first byte.

q.q: Two buildings 6 km apart need a 10 Gbps link over cable the unit owns. Which medium fits?
o: Cat 6a twisted pair
Copper Ethernet is limited to 100 m per run.
Single-mode fiber with long-range optics
Right. Single-mode fiber with LR optics carries 10 Gbps for about 10 km.
RG-6 coaxial cable
RG-6 is for cable TV and cable modems. It isn't used for a 10 Gbps Ethernet link between buildings.
Multimode OM3 fiber
OM3 reaches only about 300 m at 10 Gbps. It's built for short runs inside a building or data center.

q.q: A 90 m horizontal run from the closet to a lab must carry 10GBASE-T. Which is the lowest cable category that supports it?
o: Cat 3
Cat 3 is old voice-grade cable that tops out at 10 Mbps.
Cat 6a
Right. Cat 6a supports 10GBASE-T for the full 100 m.
Cat 6
Cat 6 handles 10GBASE-T for only about 55 m, so a 90 m run is too long.
Cat 5e
Cat 5e is rated for 1 Gbps. It isn't specified for 10GBASE-T.

q.q: Two top-of-rack switches with SFP+ ports sit 3 m apart. The team wants the cheapest 10 Gbps link that needs no separate optics. What should they buy?
o: A QSFP+ breakout cable
QSFP+ is a 40 Gbps form factor. These switches only have SFP+ ports.
A media converter
A media converter changes copper to fiber. Here both ends already take SFP+, so it isn't needed.
A direct attach copper (DAC) cable
Right. A DAC is a twinax cable with SFP+ ends built in. It's cheap and made for short runs like rack to rack.
Two SR optics and a multimode patch cable
This works, but you have to buy two transceivers plus fiber, which costs more.

q.q: A team must fit 48 duplex fiber links into a 1U patch panel. Which connector is the best fit for that density?
o: LC
Right. LC is a small form-factor connector, so many duplex pairs fit in a small panel.
SC
SC is a larger square push-pull connector. It's about twice the width of LC.
F-type
F-type is a coaxial connector for cable TV, not fiber.
ST
ST uses a round bayonet twist-lock and takes much more space per port.

q.q: A data center needs predictable, equal latency for server-to-server (east-west) traffic. Every access switch connects to every core switch, so any two servers are the same number of hops apart. Which architecture is this?
o: Collapsed core
Collapsed core merges core and distribution into one layer for smaller campuses. It doesn't promise equal hops.
Spine and leaf
Right. In spine and leaf, every leaf links to every spine, so any leaf-to-leaf path is two hops.
Three-tier
Three-tier (core, distribution, access) is built for north-south traffic. Path lengths between servers can differ.
Hub and spoke
All traffic in hub and spoke goes through one central site, which is the opposite of equal, direct paths.

q.q: Twelve small boat stations each have a single WAN link to sector headquarters. Traffic between two stations must pass through headquarters. Which topology is this?
o: Spine and leaf
Spine and leaf is a data center switching design, not a WAN layout.
Point to point
Point to point is a single link between two sites. Here twelve sites share one hub.
Full mesh
In a full mesh every site has a direct link to every other site.
Hub and spoke
Right. Every site connects only to the central hub, and spoke-to-spoke traffic goes through it.

q.q: How many links does a full mesh between 6 sites need?
o: That would be one link per site, like a ring.
Right. A full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links: 6 x 5 / 2 = 15.
There's no mesh formula that gives 12 for 6 sites.
6 x 5 = 30 counts every link twice, once from each end. Divide by 2.

q.q: A small campus can't justify separate core and distribution switches. It merges those two layers into one pair of switches above the access layer. What is this design called?
o: Spine and leaf
Spine and leaf is a data center fabric. It isn't a merged campus core.
Three-tier
Three-tier keeps core, distribution and access as separate layers.
Collapsed core
Right. A collapsed core combines the core and distribution layers into one, which saves cost in smaller networks.
Hybrid
Hybrid means mixing topologies, such as star and mesh. It doesn't specifically mean merging two layers.

q.q: Which of these addresses is a private (RFC 1918) address?
o: Right. The 172.16.0.0/12 private block runs from 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, so 172.20 is inside it.
The private block is 192.168.0.0/16. 192.169 is public.
Only 10.0.0.0/8 is private in that area. 11.x.x.x is public.
172.32 is just past the end of the private 172.16-172.31 range, so it's public.

q.q: How many usable host addresses does a /27 subnet have?
o: 27 is the prefix length, not a host count.
Right. A /27 leaves 5 host bits: 2^5 = 32 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses = 30.
32 is the total. Two of them are reserved for the network and broadcast addresses.
62 usable hosts is a /26.

q.q: The /24 network 10.20.10.0 must be split into exactly four equal subnets. Which mask should be used?
o: Right. Borrowing 2 bits gives 4 subnets of 64 addresses each (62 usable).
Borrowing 3 bits gives 8 subnets, which is double what's needed.
Borrowing 4 bits gives 16 subnets.
Borrowing 1 bit gives only 2 subnets.

q.q: Which host is in the same subnet as 192.168.14.77/27?
o: .100 is in the next block, .96-.127.
The third octet is different, so it's on another network entirely.
.63 is the broadcast address of the block before, .32-.63.
Right. /27 blocks go up in steps of 32. .77 falls in the .64-.95 block, and .90 is in it too.

q.q: A Windows laptop shows the address 169.254.33.17. Other hosts on the same VLAN have valid addresses. What does this address tell the technician?
o: The DHCP server gave it a private RFC 1918 address from the staff scope
169.254 isn't in any RFC 1918 block. DHCP wouldn't hand it out.
The laptop is using a loopback address
Loopback is 127.0.0.0/8, mostly 127.0.0.1.
The laptop has a Class D multicast address
No DHCP server answered, so it self-assigned an APIPA address
Right. 169.254.0.0/16 is APIPA (link-local). Windows uses it when no DHCP lease is received.

q.q: A command has 40 remote offices, each with an MPLS circuit and a broadband line. It wants a central controller to steer voice over the best-performing link and send bulk updates over broadband, based on app policy. What should it deploy?
o: Static routes on each branch router
Static routes are fixed. They can't change paths based on live link quality or app type.
Spanning Tree Protocol
STP blocks redundant switch links to prevent loops. It doesn't route by application.
SD-WAN
Right. SD-WAN uses a central controller to pick the WAN path for each application based on live link quality.
VXLAN
VXLAN carries Layer 2 segments over a Layer 3 network inside a data center. It doesn't pick WAN paths by app.

q.q: A data center has run out of VLAN IDs and needs to extend Layer 2 segments across a routed Layer 3 network. Which technology fits?
o: VXLAN
Right. VXLAN wraps Layer 2 frames in UDP and uses a 24-bit ID, which allows about 16 million segments.
Link aggregation (LACP)
LACP bundles physical links together. It doesn't add segments or cross a routed network.
802.1Q trunking
802.1Q uses a 12-bit VLAN ID, so it's capped at 4,094 VLANs. That's the limit they already hit.
SD-WAN
SD-WAN steers branch WAN traffic. It doesn't stretch Layer 2 inside a data center.

q.q: A new policy says being on the office LAN earns no trust. Every request to an app is checked against the user's identity, the device's health and context, every time. Which model is this?
o: Zero trust architecture
Right. Zero trust gives no implicit trust based on location. Every access request is verified.
Split-tunnel VPN
Split tunneling decides which traffic goes through a VPN. It doesn't verify each request.
Perimeter (castle-and-moat) security
Perimeter security trusts whatever is inside the network, which is exactly what this policy rejects.
A screened subnet (DMZ)
A DMZ is a zone for public-facing servers. It isn't a policy of checking every request.

q.q: A command wants one cloud service that combines SD-WAN with a secure web gateway, CASB, zero trust network access and firewall as a service, for both branch offices and roaming users. What is this approach called?
o: IaaS
IaaS rents out compute, storage and network. It doesn't include these security services.
VPC
A VPC is your private network inside a cloud provider.
NFV
NFV runs network functions as software. It isn't a single cloud service that bundles them.
SASE
Right. Secure Access Service Edge joins WAN networking and cloud-delivered security in one service.

q.q: A router has three routes: 10.20.0.0/16 learned by OSPF, 10.20.30.0/24 as a static route, and 10.20.30.128/25 learned by EIGRP. Which route is used for a packet to 10.20.30.200?
o: The OSPF /16, because it covers the whole network
The /16 matches, but it's the least specific match, so it loses.
The static /24, because static routes have the lowest administrative distance
Administrative distance only breaks ties between routes for the same prefix length. A longer prefix always wins first.
The default route, because no route matches exactly
Three routes match. A default route is only used when nothing more specific does.
The EIGRP /25
Right. Routers choose the longest prefix match first. 10.20.30.200 falls in 10.20.30.128/25, the most specific route that matches.

q.q: A router learns 172.16.40.0/24 from both OSPF and internal EIGRP, using default settings. Which route goes in the routing table, and why?
o: EIGRP, because its AD of 90 beats OSPF's 110
Right. When the prefix is identical, the lower administrative distance wins. Internal EIGRP is 90 and OSPF is 110.
Both, load-balanced equally
Equal-cost load balancing happens within one protocol. Between protocols, only the lower AD route gets installed.
OSPF, because link-state protocols are always preferred
Protocol type doesn't decide this. Administrative distance does, and OSPF's is higher.
Whichever protocol calculated the lower metric for the route
OSPF cost and EIGRP metric are on different scales and can't be compared. That's why AD is used.

q.q: A unit's border router must exchange routes with two internet providers, and each organization is a separate autonomous system. Which routing protocol is built for this?
o: BGP
Right. BGP is the exterior gateway protocol for routing between autonomous systems, including multi-homing to ISPs.
RIP
RIP is an old interior protocol with a 15-hop limit. It isn't used for internet routing.
EIGRP
EIGRP is also an interior protocol and isn't used between providers.
OSPF
OSPF is an interior protocol, used inside one organization's network.

q.q: Two hundred workstations must reach the internet through one public IP address. The router tells the sessions apart by translating source port numbers. What is this called?
o: Dynamic NAT with a pool
Dynamic NAT still maps one-to-one, just from a pool. It would run out with one public address.
PAT (NAT overload)
Right. Port address translation maps many private addresses to one public address, using unique source ports to track each session.
A first hop redundancy protocol
FHRP keeps the default gateway available. It doesn't translate addresses.
Static NAT
Static NAT is a fixed one-to-one mapping, so it would need 200 public addresses.

q.q: Hosts point to 10.20.10.1 as their default gateway. The unit has two routers and wants hosts to keep working if one router fails, without changing any host settings. What should be configured?
o: OSPF between the routers
OSPF shares routes between routers. Hosts still point to one fixed gateway address.
An FHRP such as VRRP or HSRP, using 10.20.10.1 as the virtual IP
Right. With FHRP, two routers share one virtual IP, and the standby takes it over if the active router fails.
A second default gateway added to every host's IP settings by GPO
Most hosts don't fail over cleanly between gateways, and it means changing every host.
Spanning Tree Protocol on both routers
STP prevents switching loops. It doesn't share a gateway address.

q.q: Voice calls get choppy every night when backups saturate the WAN link. The team can't add bandwidth this year. Which change best protects the calls?
o: Shorten DHCP lease times
DHCP leases have nothing to do with WAN congestion.
Increase the MTU on the phones
Voice packets are small. A bigger MTU doesn't stop backups from crowding them out.
QoS: mark voice as DSCP EF and give it a priority queue
Right. QoS puts voice ahead of bulk traffic, so the calls keep low delay and jitter during congestion.
Enable jumbo frames on the WAN interfaces so backups finish faster
Bigger frames don't reprioritize anything, and the WAN path may not support them.

q.q: A ceiling AP broadcasts a staff SSID mapped to VLAN 10 and a guest SSID mapped to VLAN 20. How should its switch port be set up?
o: As an 802.1Q trunk that allows VLANs 10 and 20
Right. One cable has to carry two VLANs, so the port must be a trunk that tags frames for both.
As an access port in VLAN 20
Same problem: staff traffic couldn't be carried.
As a routed port with a subinterface for each SSID
The AP bridges SSIDs to VLANs. The switch needs a trunk, not a routed interface.
As an access port in VLAN 10
An access port carries just one untagged VLAN, so guest traffic would have no path.

q.q: User-facing access ports should start forwarding as soon as a PC connects, and should shut down if anyone plugs in a switch that sends BPDUs. Which pair of features does this?
o: PortFast and BPDU guard
Right. PortFast skips the STP listening and learning delay. BPDU guard err-disables the port as soon as it receives a BPDU.
Port security and storm control
Port security limits MAC addresses, and storm control caps broadcast rates. Neither reacts to BPDUs.
Root guard and loop guard
Root guard blocks superior BPDUs on designated ports without shutting the port down, and loop guard protects blocked ports. Neither speeds up edge ports.
LACP and 802.1Q
These bundle links and tag VLANs. They don't change STP behavior on edge ports.

q.q: Three switches run STP with default settings, except SW3, which has bridge priority 28672. SW1 has the lowest MAC address. Which switch becomes the root bridge?
o: SW3
Right. The root is the lowest bridge ID, and priority is compared before MAC. 28672 beats the default 32768.
SW2
Nothing makes SW2 better than the others on priority or MAC.
Whichever switch booted first
Boot order plays no part in root bridge election.
SW1
MAC address only breaks a tie when priorities are equal. Here they aren't.

q.q: Two 10 Gbps links between a pair of switches should act as one 20 Gbps logical link and keep working if one cable fails. Which standard negotiates this?
o: IEEE 802.3at
802.3at is PoE+.
IEEE 802.1X
802.1X is port-based network access control.
LACP (IEEE 802.3ad / 802.1AX)
Right. LACP bundles physical links into one port channel and drops a failed member automatically.
IEEE 802.1Q
802.1Q tags VLANs on a trunk. It doesn't bundle links.

q.q: After jumbo frames (9000-byte MTU) were turned on for a storage server's NICs and its access switch, small file copies work but large transfers stall. What is the most likely cause?
o: Jumbo frames need half duplex
Jumbo frames are a full-duplex Ethernet feature. Half duplex has nothing to do with it.
Spanning tree is putting the storage port into blocking during large transfers
A blocked port would stop all traffic, not just the large transfers.
The VLAN needs a new ID
The VLAN ID doesn't affect frame size.
A device on the path, such as the array or an uplink, is still at 1500 MTU
Right. Every hop and endpoint must use the same MTU. Large frames get dropped where the MTU is smaller.

q.q: A switch port in a public lobby should accept only the kiosk's MAC address and shut down if any other device is connected. Which feature does this?
o: BPDU guard
BPDU guard only reacts to switches sending BPDUs. A laptop wouldn't trigger it.
Port security: maximum 1 MAC, violation mode shutdown
Right. Port security limits and learns allowed MAC addresses, and shutdown mode err-disables the port on a violation.
A VLAN access control list (VACL) that permits only the kiosk's IP
A VACL filters traffic by address or protocol. It doesn't shut a port when a new device appears.
PortFast
PortFast only speeds up the move to forwarding.

q.q: A new Wi-Fi 6 AP needs about 25 W, but the closet switch only supports 802.3af. What will most likely happen when the AP is connected?
o: The AP draws extra power over the data pairs and runs normally
PoE power comes from the switch. Other pairs can't create extra wattage.
It won't get enough power. It needs 802.3at (PoE+) or better.
Right. 802.3af supplies up to 15.4 W per port. PoE+ supplies up to 30 W, which covers 25 W.
The AP works, but only on 2.4 GHz, with no other effect
Some APs do reduce features on low power, but it isn't guaranteed. The real issue is that the switch can't supply 25 W.
The switch automatically upgrades the port to PoE+
Hardware limits power. A port can't deliver more than its standard allows.

q.q: Three APs in a row cover a hallway on the 2.4 GHz band. Which channel plan avoids overlap between them?
o: Right. In the US, channels 1, 6 and 11 are the only three that don't overlap in 2.4 GHz.
1, 2 and 3
Neighboring channels are only 5 MHz apart, so these overlap heavily.
3, 6 and 9
Each 20 MHz channel overlaps with channels 3 numbers away.
1, 5 and 9
They're still 4 channels apart, which isn't enough. 1, 6 and 11 are the standard set.

q.q: A visitor center wants a guest Wi-Fi network with no password, but each visitor's traffic must still be encrypted over the air. Which option fits?
o: WPA2-Personal with the passphrase on a sign
It needs a passphrase, and anyone who has it plus the handshake can decrypt other visitors' traffic.
Wi-Fi Enhanced Open (OWE)
Right. Opportunistic Wireless Encryption, usually deployed alongside WPA3, gives each client its own encryption on an open network, with no shared password.
WEP with a posted key
WEP is broken, and it needs a key.
An open SSID with MAC filtering
MAC filtering doesn't encrypt anything, and MAC addresses are easy to spoof.

q.q: Each staff member must sign in to the Wi-Fi with their own directory account, and access must be revoked as soon as their account is disabled. Which setup does this?
o: WPA3-Personal with SAE
Personal mode uses one shared passphrase, not per-user accounts.
WPA3-Enterprise using 802.1X and RADIUS
Right. Enterprise mode authenticates each user against a central server, so disabling the account blocks Wi-Fi access.
A hidden SSID
Hiding the SSID doesn't authenticate anyone, and the network is still easy to find.
MAC address filtering with a list of staff devices
MAC filtering ties access to the device, not the user account, and it's easy to spoof.

q.q: Voice-over-Wi-Fi calls drop for a moment whenever users walk between APs on the same SSID. Which feature should be enabled?
o: A hidden SSID
Hiding the SSID has no effect on roaming speed.
Channel bonding to 80 MHz
Wider channels add throughput, but they don't make handoffs faster. They can even cause more interference.
802.11r fast BSS transition
Right. 802.11r caches keys, so a client can roam to a new AP without a full re-authentication.
802.11h handles dynamic frequency selection and transmit power control. It doesn't speed up roaming.

q.q: Two buildings 2 km apart with clear line of sight need a wireless bridge. Which antennas should be used?
o: Omnidirectional antennas
Omnis spread signal in every direction, which wastes power and limits range.
Any antennas, with transmit power at maximum
Raising power without directional gain usually goes over regulatory limits and still falls short.
Directional antennas (parabolic or Yagi) aimed at each other
Right. Directional antennas focus energy into a narrow beam, which gives the gain a long point-to-point link needs.
Ceiling-mount APs with internal antennas on each building's roof
These are built to cover rooms, not a 2 km link.

q.q: A wireless survey shows two APs both advertising the network name CG-Guest. What uniquely identifies each AP's radio?
o: The channel number
Two APs can use the same channel, so the channel doesn't identify a radio.
The ESSID
The ESSID (extended service set) is the shared network made up of both APs.
The SSID
The SSID is the network name, and both APs share it.
The BSSID
Right. The BSSID is the radio's MAC address, so it's unique to each AP radio.

q.q: A core switch has two power supplies. How should they be connected for the best resilience?
o: One supply plugged in now, the other left unplugged as a cold spare
A disconnected supply gives no protection when the active one fails.
Each supply to a different PDU on a separate circuit (A/B feeds)
Right. Separate feeds mean that losing one circuit, PDU or UPS still leaves the switch powered.
Both supplies to a single surge protector
That's still one point of failure, and it doesn't protect against an outage.
Both supplies to the same PDU
One PDU or breaker failure would cut both supplies at once.

q.q: Server racks in a small room are overheating because hot exhaust is going back into equipment inlets. Which layout change helps most?
o: Turn every other rack around so their fronts face the opposite direction
That points one rack's exhaust into the next rack's intake, which makes it worse.
Remove the side panels from the racks
Open sides let hot air circulate more.
Add more cable management in the front of the racks
Cable bundles in front can block intake airflow.
Use hot and cold aisles and fill empty rack spaces with blanking panels
Right. Inlets facing a shared cold aisle and exhausts facing a hot aisle keep the air streams apart. Blanking panels stop hot air from looping back.

q.q: A new wing's farthest office is 130 m of cable path from the main closet (MDF). What is the best design?
o: Install an IDF closer to the wing with a fiber uplink to the MDF
Right. Copper Ethernet is limited to 100 m per channel. An IDF with a fiber uplink keeps every copper run in spec.
Lower the link speed to 10 Mbps for extra distance
The 100 m limit applies at every speed.
Put an unmanaged switch above the ceiling at the halfway point
That works electrically, but it's unmanaged, unsecured and hard to service.
Use Cat 6a so the run can reach 130 m
No cable category goes past the 100 m channel limit.

q.q: A technician needs to find which patch panel port and switch port connect to wall jack 214-B. Which document should they check?
o: The cable map / physical diagram with patch panel labeling
Right. Physical documentation and labels trace every jack through the patch panel to a switch port.
The service-level agreement
An SLA defines promised service levels. It has nothing about wiring.
The IP address management (IPAM) database
IPAM tracks address assignments, not cable paths.
The logical network diagram
A logical diagram shows subnets, VLANs and routing, not individual jacks.

q.q: Two project teams set up the same /24 for different sites, and an outage followed. Which tool would most directly prevent this?
o: A baseline configuration
A baseline is a standard device configuration. It doesn't coordinate subnet use between teams.
IP address management (IPAM)
Right. IPAM tracks which subnets and addresses are in use, so overlapping assignments get caught before deployment.
An asset inventory
An asset inventory tracks hardware and licenses, not address space.
A rack diagram
A rack diagram shows where equipment is mounted.

q.q: A WAN router's firmware bug is causing an outage right now, and the fix can't wait for next week's change board. How should the change be handled?
o: Wait for the next scheduled change board meeting
Waiting leaves the mission down when an emergency process exists for exactly this.
Roll back every change made in the past week, then wait for the board to approve a new fix
Rolling back unrelated changes with no analysis can cause new outages.
Apply it without any approval or record, since it's an emergency
Skipping documentation breaks change control and makes the next outage harder to investigate.
Treat it as an emergency change: expedited approval, apply it, document and review after
Right. Emergency changes still need authorization and records. The process is just faster.

q.q: A team wants to spot when any switch's settings drift from the approved standard. What should the running configs be compared against?
o: Yesterday's backup configuration
A backup only shows changes since yesterday, and it may already contain drift.
The baseline configuration
Right. The baseline is the approved standard, so differences from it show drift.
The vendor's factory default configuration
Factory defaults aren't the approved standard and usually aren't secure.
The production configuration
Production is the running config itself, the thing you're checking.

q.q: The vendor announces that a switch model has reached end of support (EOS). The switches work fine today. What is the main risk of keeping them?
o: The switches stop forwarding traffic on the EOS date
EOS ends support, not function. The switches keep running.
The switches can no longer be monitored with SNMP
SNMP still works. The risk is security and supportability.
No more security patches or vendor support for new flaws
Right. EOS means the vendor stops patching and supporting it, even if the hardware still runs.
The vendor revokes the switch licenses and the ports go unlicensed
EOS doesn't revoke licenses. The issue is no updates or support.

q.q: A network management system must poll switches with both authentication and encryption. Which setup meets this?
o: SNMPv1 with read-only access
SNMPv1 has no encryption and only weak, clear-text authentication.
SNMPv3 with authPriv
Right. SNMPv3 in authPriv mode authenticates messages and encrypts them.
SNMPv3 with noAuthNoPriv
That mode uses neither authentication nor encryption.
SNMPv2c with a long community string
Community strings travel in clear text and give no encryption.

q.q: Leaders want a weekly report of which hosts and applications use the most WAN bandwidth. They don't need packet contents. Which data source fits best?
o: SNMP interface counters
Counters show how busy a link is, not which hosts or apps caused it.
Full packet capture on the WAN link
Capturing every packet would work, but it's huge, slow to search, and collects contents that aren't needed.
Syslog from the routers
Syslog records events, not per-conversation traffic volumes.
Flow data (NetFlow / IPFIX)
Right. Flow records summarize who talked to whom, on which ports, and how much, without storing payloads.

q.q: A new IDS needs a copy of every frame going in and out of the firewall's switch port, without being placed inline. What should be configured on the switch?
o: Port mirroring (SPAN) from the firewall port to the IDS port
Right. SPAN copies frames from one or more ports to a monitor port, so the IDS sees them without being inline.
PoE on the IDS port
PoE delivers power, not traffic.
An LACP bundle with the firewall
LACP bundles links for capacity. It doesn't make copies for monitoring.
Port security on the IDS port
Port security limits MAC addresses. It doesn't copy traffic.

q.q: A WAN link hits 75% use every weekday morning when staff sign in, and the fixed 70% alert fires daily. What is the best way to alert only on unusual load?
o: Poll the link less often so the morning peak is averaged out of the graph
Polling less often only hides detail. It doesn't define what's normal.
Turn off the alert
Then real problems would go unseen.
Raise the threshold to 100%
At 100% the link is already saturated, so the alert comes too late.
Baseline normal use by time of day and alert on deviations
Right. A baseline shows what's normal, so alerts fire on real anomalies instead of the daily peak.

q.q: A collector is set to keep syslog messages at severity critical (2) and anything more severe. Which levels does it keep?
o: Critical (2), error (3) and warning (4)
Those are critical and less severe. Higher numbers mean less severe.
Emergency (0), alert (1) and critical (2)
Right. Lower syslog numbers are more severe, so critical and above means 0, 1 and 2.
Only critical (2)
"And more severe" also includes 0 and 1.
Debugging (7) through critical (2)
That range is everything from critical down to the least severe.

q.q: A dispatch system can lose no more than 15 minutes of data and must be back in service within 4 hours of an outage. How are these targets labeled?
o: RTO 15 minutes, RPO 4 hours
The labels are swapped. Data loss is RPO and downtime is RTO.
MTTR 15 minutes, MTBF 4 hours
MTTR and MTBF describe repair time and how reliable equipment is, not recovery targets.
RPO 15 minutes, RTO 4 hours
Right. RPO is how much data loss is acceptable. RTO is how long until service must be restored.
MTBF 15 minutes, RTO 4 hours
MTBF is the average time between failures, not data loss.

q.q: A recovery site has equipment installed and data copied continuously, and it can take over within minutes. Which type of site is it?
o: Hot site
Right. A hot site is fully equipped with current data, ready to run almost immediately.
Active-passive cluster in the same room
That's local redundancy, not a separate recovery site.
Cold site
A cold site has only space, power and cooling, so recovery takes days to weeks.
Warm site
A warm site has hardware but older data, so recovery takes hours to days.

q.q: Firewall A has an MTBF of 80,000 hours and an MTTR of 24 hours. Firewall B has an MTBF of 60,000 hours and an MTTR of 2 hours. Which gives higher availability?
o: Firewall A, because it fails less often
It fails less often, but each failure lasts 24 hours, so total downtime is higher.
Firewall B, since its faster repairs outweigh its lower MTBF
They're equal, because both have better than 99% availability
Both are over 99%, but B has about ten times less downtime.
You can't tell without the RPO
RPO is about data loss. Availability comes from MTBF and MTTR.

q.q: Two firewalls in an active-active pair each run at about 70% load. One fails. What happens?
o: The standby unit takes over at 70%
There's no idle standby in active-active. Both were already carrying traffic.
Traffic drops by half on purpose
The pair doesn't throttle traffic on its own. The survivor is simply overloaded.
Nothing changes, because active-active hides failures
Failover works, but the load still has to fit on the remaining unit.
The survivor gets about 140% of its capacity and becomes overloaded
Right. In active-active, each unit must stay under about 50% load, or the survivor can't absorb the other's traffic.

q.q: A capture shows a client getting offers from two DHCP servers, then broadcasting a DHCPREQUEST that names one server. What does that REQUEST do?
o: It accepts one offer and tells the other server its offer wasn't taken
Right. The REQUEST is broadcast and names the chosen server, so both servers learn the outcome.
It asks both servers to assign the address together
Only one server's lease is accepted.
It renews an existing lease
Renewals are unicast to the leasing server. This is the third step of DORA after offers.
It reports an address conflict
Conflicts are reported with DHCPDECLINE, not REQUEST.

q.q: Clients in VLAN 30 get APIPA addresses. The DHCP server is in the server VLAN and has a valid scope for VLAN 30. What is most likely missing?
o: A DNS forwarder on the DHCP server for VLAN 30
DNS forwarding is about name resolution, not getting an address.
A DHCP reservation for each client
Reservations fix addresses for specific devices. They don't help a broadcast reach another subnet.
A longer lease time
Lease length doesn't matter if requests never reach the server.
A DHCP relay (IP helper) on VLAN 30's gateway
Right. DHCP Discover is a broadcast, and routers don't forward broadcasts. A relay forwards it to the server as unicast.

q.q: A network printer must always get 10.20.10.50 but should stay managed by DHCP, so its gateway and DNS settings update automatically. What should be configured?
o: An exclusion range that contains 10.20.10.50
An exclusion stops DHCP from handing out the address at all.
A DHCP reservation for the printer's MAC address
Right. A reservation always gives that MAC the same IP, and the printer still receives DHCP options.
An infinite lease for every client
That doesn't tie the address to the printer and wastes the pool.
A static IP typed on the printer
That works, but it leaves DHCP management, so option changes won't reach the printer.

q.q: To cut spoofed email, the unit must publish which servers may send mail for its domain (SPF). Which DNS record type holds this?
o: MX
MX records say which servers receive mail, not which may send it.
CNAME
A CNAME makes one name an alias for another. It doesn't hold policy text.
TXT
Right. SPF policies are published as TXT records on the domain.
PTR
PTR records map an IP back to a name for reverse lookups.

q.q: Domain sign-ins fail on several servers, and log timestamps don't match across devices by several minutes. What should be fixed first?
o: NTP: sync every device to the same time source
Right. Kerberos rejects tickets when clocks drift past the allowed skew (5 minutes by default), and logs can't be correlated. NTP uses UDP 123.
DNS PTR records
Missing PTR records break reverse lookups, not clock-sensitive authentication.
The SNMP community strings on the domain controllers
SNMP settings don't keep clocks in sync.
DHCP lease times
Leases don't affect clock accuracy.

q.q: An IPv6 host gets its prefix from a router advertisement and builds its own address with no DHCPv6 server. What is this called?
o: Stateful DHCPv6
Stateful DHCPv6 needs a server to assign and track the address.
APIPA
APIPA is IPv4's 169.254 fallback when DHCP fails.
NAT64
NAT64 translates between IPv6 and IPv4. It doesn't assign addresses.
SLAAC
Right. Stateless address autoconfiguration uses the advertised prefix plus a host-generated interface ID.

q.q: A bad config change cut off all in-band access to a remote router. How can admins still reach it?
o: SSH to its management IP
SSH is in-band, and in-band access is what's lost.
Out-of-band access through its console port
Right. A console server or cellular modem on the console port is out-of-band: it doesn't depend on the production network, so it still works when that network is down.
An SNMP set command from the NMS
SNMP also uses the broken production network.
The HTTPS web interface, reached from a different subnet
The web interface is in-band too.

q.q: Policy says every remote user's internet traffic, not just traffic to unit servers, must pass through headquarters' security stack. Which VPN setting enforces this?
o: Site-to-site VPN
Site-to-site links two networks. It isn't how individual remote users connect.
Full tunnel
Right. A full tunnel sends all of the client's traffic through the VPN, including internet browsing.
Clientless (browser) VPN
A clientless portal only publishes certain web apps. It doesn't carry all traffic.
Split tunnel
A split tunnel sends only internal traffic through the VPN. Internet traffic goes out locally.

q.q: Admins must reach servers in a protected subnet, and only one hardened, heavily logged host may accept their SSH connections. What is that host called?
o: A domain controller
A domain controller authenticates users. It isn't meant as an SSH gateway.
A proxy server
A web proxy handles HTTP traffic for users. It isn't an admin access point.
A honeypot
A honeypot is a decoy meant to attract attackers.
A jump box (bastion host)
Right. A jump box is the single controlled entry point. Admins connect to it first, then on to the servers.

q.q: The network team needs AAA for router logins: separate authorization of each command and encryption of the whole AAA payload. Which protocol fits?
o: SAML
SAML handles web single sign-on with signed assertions, not CLI sessions on routers.
LDAP
LDAP is a directory protocol. It doesn't authorize individual router commands.
TACACS+
Right. TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization and accounting, can authorize each command, and encrypts the whole payload.
RADIUS
RADIUS combines authentication and authorization and only encrypts the password field. It's the common choice for network access, not device admin.

q.q: Users sign in once at the unit portal, and several cloud web apps then accept them using signed assertions from the identity provider. Which standard does this?
o: RADIUS
RADIUS mostly authenticates network access such as Wi-Fi and VPN, not browser SSO to cloud apps.
TACACS+
TACACS+ is for administrator access to network devices.
SNMPv3
SNMPv3 is for network monitoring, not user sign-in.
SAML
Right. SAML passes signed XML assertions from an identity provider to service providers for web single sign-on.

q.q: A laptop's drive must stay unreadable if the laptop is stolen, and the user's sessions to unit web apps must be protected on hotel Wi-Fi. Which pair covers both?
o: Full-disk encryption for both
Disk encryption doesn't protect traffic once it leaves the laptop.
Full-disk encryption (at rest) and TLS (in transit)
Right. Disk encryption protects stored data. TLS protects data while it crosses the network.
Hashing both the disk contents and the web traffic with SHA-256
Hashing proves integrity, but it doesn't hide data from a thief or eavesdropper.
TLS for both
TLS protects connections. It does nothing for the files on the disk.

q.q: Cameras recorded someone tailgating into the network closet, but nobody was stopped. What type of control did the cameras act as?
o: Preventive
Preventive controls such as locks or vestibules stop entry. The person still got in.
Detective
Right. The cameras recorded the event so it could be found and investigated. They didn't stop it, which makes them detective.
Corrective
Corrective controls fix things after an incident, like restoring from backup.
Compensating
Compensating controls stand in for a primary control that can't be used.

q.q: Building cameras, HVAC controllers and badge readers share a flat network with the finance servers. Which change best reduces the risk these IoT/OT devices pose?
o: Turn on QoS for the IoT traffic
QoS manages priority. It doesn't restrict access.
Segment them into their own VLAN with firewall rules for needed flows only
Right. Segmentation keeps a compromised device from reaching unrelated systems.
Give each device a static IP address in the finance subnet so they're tracked
That keeps them on the same flat network.
Change their DNS servers
DNS settings don't control which systems a device can reach.

q.q: A unit processes card payments at its exchange store. Which standard governs protecting that cardholder data?
o: Data locality
Data locality is about where data is physically stored. It isn't a card security standard.
GDPR
GDPR is the EU's personal data protection law. It isn't specific to card data.
PCI DSS
Right. The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard applies to any organization that stores, processes or sends cardholder data.
ISO 9001
ISO 9001 is about quality management.

q.q: Security deploys a fake file server with no real data that logs everything an intruder does on it, to learn their methods. What is this?
o: A honeypot
Right. A honeypot is a decoy system built to attract and record attacker activity.
A sinkhole
A DNS sinkhole redirects bad domains. It isn't a fake server for intruders to explore.
A jump box
A jump box is a real, hardened admin entry point.
A screened subnet
A screened subnet (DMZ) hosts real public-facing services.

q.q: An attacker sends small DNS queries with the victim's spoofed source IP to thousands of open resolvers, and the large answers flood the victim's link. What is this attack?
o: DNS cache poisoning
Poisoning plants false records in a resolver to redirect users. It doesn't flood anyone.
A DNS amplification (reflection) DDoS
Right. Spoofed queries make resolvers send much larger replies to the victim, multiplying the attack traffic.
DNS tunneling
Tunneling hides data inside DNS queries to sneak it out of a network.
A SYN flood
A SYN flood abuses TCP handshakes. This attack abuses DNS replies over UDP.

q.q: Users on a VLAN get certificate warnings. On an affected PC, arp -a shows the gateway's IP mapped to the MAC of another workstation. What attack is likely?
o: ARP spoofing to put the attacker on-path
Right. Fake ARP replies point the gateway's IP at the attacker's MAC, so traffic flows through the attacker.
DHCP starvation
Starvation uses up leases. It doesn't rewrite ARP caches.
MAC flooding
MAC flooding fills the switch's table. It doesn't change a host's ARP entry for the gateway.
VLAN hopping
VLAN hopping reaches another VLAN. Here the attacker is on the same VLAN.

q.q: An attacker on an access port in the native VLAN sends frames with two 802.1Q tags and reaches a host in another VLAN. Which attack is this, and what helps prevent it?
o: Double-tagging VLAN hopping; fix by not putting users in the native VLAN
Right. The first switch strips the outer native tag, and the next switch forwards on the inner tag. Use an unused VLAN as the native VLAN and keep users out of it.
An evil twin. Enable WPA3.
Evil twins are a wireless attack. This happened on a wired trunk path.
MAC flooding. Enable PortFast.
PortFast only speeds up STP. Neither part fits.
ARP spoofing; fix by enabling DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection on the VLAN
This attack works with VLAN tags, not ARP.

q.q: Staff in the parking lot see a strong "CG-Staff" network, connect, and get a login page asking for their network credentials. The real staff Wi-Fi uses 802.1X with no web login. What is this?
o: Wardriving
Wardriving is driving around mapping Wi-Fi networks. It doesn't set up a fake one.
Jamming
Jamming drowns out the signal. It doesn't present a fake login page.
An evil twin (rogue AP)
Right. An attacker's AP copies a trusted SSID to trick users into connecting and handing over credentials.
Bluejacking
Bluejacking sends unwanted messages over Bluetooth.

q.q: An attacker floods a switch with frames from thousands of fake source MACs. The MAC table fills, and the switch starts sending unicast frames out every port. What attack is this, and what stops it?
o: A broadcast storm. Enable PortFast.
A storm comes from a loop. PortFast would make a loop worse.
ARP spoofing. Turn off ARP.
ARP can't be turned off, and this attack targets the switch's table, not ARP caches.
MAC flooding. Port security limits MACs per port.
Right. Filling the CAM table makes the switch flood traffic like a hub, so the attacker can capture it. Port security caps learned MACs.
DNS poisoning. Use DNSSEC.
DNS has no part in a switch's MAC table.

q.q: Which switch feature checks ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table and drops ones that don't match?
o: Storm control
Storm control caps broadcast rates, but it can't tell real ARP from fake.
Port security
Port security limits MACs per port. It doesn't validate ARP contents.
Dynamic ARP inspection (DAI)
Right. DAI checks each ARP packet's IP-to-MAC pair against the snooping bindings to block ARP spoofing.
BPDU guard
BPDU guard reacts to spanning tree BPDUs, not ARP.

q.q: An ACL reads, in order: 1) permit tcp any host 10.20.30.5 eq 443, 2) deny ip any any log, 3) permit tcp 10.20.10.0/24 host 10.20.30.5 eq 22. Admins in 10.20.10.0/24 still can't SSH to the server. Why?
o: Line 1 blocks SSH because it already names the same destination host
Line 1 only matches port 443, so SSH doesn't match it.
ACLs run top-down, so line 2 denies SSH before line 3
Right. The first match wins. The SSH permit has to come before the deny-all.
SSH uses UDP 22, not TCP
SSH runs over TCP 22.
ACLs need a reboot to take effect
ACL changes apply right away on network devices.

q.q: New switches arrive with admin/admin credentials, plus Telnet and HTTP management turned on. Which TWO actions harden them before deployment? (Choose two.)
o: Leave defaults until monitoring is set up
Every day on defaults is open exposure.
Turn on every unused switch port for future growth
Unused ports should be disabled, not enabled.
Enable SNMPv1 with the community string public
SNMPv1 with a default community string adds an insecure management path.
Change the default credentials to unique, strong ones
Right. Default credentials are published and are among the first things attackers try.
Disable Telnet and HTTP and manage the switches over SSH and HTTPS
Right. Telnet and HTTP send credentials in clear text. SSH and HTTPS encrypt the session.

q.q: Only unit-managed, patched laptops may join the wired network. Anything else must be put into a remediation VLAN automatically. What should be deployed?
o: Port security with sticky MACs
Sticky MACs remember devices, but they don't check patch level or move devices to a remediation VLAN.
NAC using 802.1X with posture assessment
Right. Network access control checks identity and device health at connection time and assigns a VLAN based on the result.
A captive portal on the wired ports
A captive portal gathers a login or terms acceptance. It doesn't check whether a device is patched.
MAC filtering on the DHCP server
MAC filtering is easy to spoof and doesn't check device health.

q.q: An audit finds 30 unused wall jacks across the building with live switch ports behind them. What is the best fix?
o: Turn on PortFast on those ports
PortFast speeds up access. It doesn't restrict it.
Turn on PoE on those ports
PoE just supplies power.
Label the jacks as unused and note them in the cable map
Labels don't stop anyone from plugging in.
Shut the unused ports and park them in an unused VLAN
Right. Disabled ports in a dead VLAN mean that plugging in gives no network access.

q.q: A technician has questioned users, found the symptoms, and learned that a switch was replaced last night. They suspect the new switch's uplink is in the wrong VLAN. What is the next step in the troubleshooting methodology?
o: Establish a plan of action and identify potential effects
Planning comes after the theory is confirmed.
Document findings, actions and outcomes
Documentation is the final step.
Test the theory to determine the cause
Right. After establishing a theory of probable cause, the next step is testing it before changing anything.
Verify full system functionality
You verify after you put a fix in place.

q.q: A tech's test shows the theory was wrong: the uplink VLAN is correct. What should happen next?
o: Establish a new theory, or escalate
Right. When a theory isn't confirmed, the methodology says to form a new one or escalate.
Implement the original fix anyway
Changing something you've shown isn't the cause adds risk and doesn't fix the problem.
Document the problem as resolved
It isn't resolved.
Go back and question the users again
Gathering more information can help a new theory, but the defined next step is a new theory or escalation.

q.q: A fix restored connectivity for one floor. Before closing the ticket, what should the technician do?
o: Close the ticket right away, since the users confirmed it works
Other systems may still be affected, and documentation is still due.
Identify the problem by gathering more information
That's the first step, not the last.
Verify full system functionality and add preventive measures
Right. Make sure everything works, not just the original symptom, and prevent a repeat.
Re-establish a theory of probable cause
The cause is already confirmed and fixed.

q.q: In the identify-the-problem step, users report slow Wi-Fi, a printer that's offline, and failed VPN logins all at once. What does the methodology recommend?
o: Approach multiple problems individually
Right. Treat each problem on its own unless the evidence links them, so one doesn't hide the others.
Skip to documenting the issues
Documentation comes at the end.
Escalate all three right away
Escalation comes after theories fail or the issue is beyond your scope.
Assume one root cause and reboot the core switch
Guessing at one cause and making a big change adds risk.

q.q: A link shows heavy slowdowns. One side is set to auto-negotiate and the other is hard-coded to 100 Mbps full duplex. The auto side reports late collisions. What is the problem?
o: Crosstalk from a damaged cable
Crosstalk causes CRC errors, but the pattern of late collisions plus mixed settings points to duplex.
A duplex mismatch: the auto side fell back to half duplex
Right. When negotiation fails, the auto side picks half duplex, which causes late collisions on that side and CRC errors on the other.
A speed mismatch: the link can't come up
The link is up. The speed matched, and the duplex didn't.
Wrong VLAN assignment
A VLAN problem stops reachability. It doesn't cause collisions.

q.q: A new 10G link between two buildings runs over single-mode fiber. One end has an LR optic, the other an SR optic. The link stays down. What is the cause?
o: The switch needs PoE turned on
PoE has nothing to do with fiber.
Mismatched optics: SR is multimode (850 nm), LR is single-mode (1310 nm)
Right. Both ends need the same optic type and wavelength to match the fiber.
The fiber strands need to be crossed over, swapping transmit and receive at one end
Duplex LC patch cords already handle transmit and receive. Swapping them doesn't fix mismatched optics.
Single-mode fiber can't carry 10G
Single-mode carries 10G over long distances.

q.q: A new copper run passes a basic continuity (wire map) test, but certification shows heavy near-end crosstalk, and the link has errors. What is the most likely wiring fault?
o: A short between pins 1 and 2
A short would also fail the wire map.
A split pair
Right. Each pin connects to the right pin at the far end, but the wires come from different twisted pairs, so the twist doesn't cancel crosstalk.
A crossover cable
A crossover shows up as a distinct pin mapping on a wire map. It doesn't hide as a pass.
An open on pin 3
An open would fail continuity.

q.q: A UTP run that passes along a machinery room next to large motors gets intermittent CRC errors that get worse when the equipment runs. What is the best fix?
o: Turn on jumbo frames
Bigger frames make each error cost more.
Replace the switch
The switch isn't causing the noise.
Hard-code both ends of the link to 10 Mbps half duplex to reduce errors
Slowing the link hides the problem and adds duplex risk.
Reroute it away from the motors, or use shielded cable or fiber
Right. The motors put out EMI. Distance, shielding or fiber removes the noise.

q.q: A 4 km fiber between two sites has gone dark. Which tool finds the distance to the break?
o: An optical time-domain reflectometer (OTDR)
Right. An OTDR sends light pulses down the fiber and times the reflections to locate breaks and bad splices.
A light meter
A light meter shows that power is lost, but not where along the fiber it's lost.
A TDR
A TDR does the same job for copper cable, not fiber.
A tone generator and probe
A toner traces copper cables through walls. It can't measure fiber faults.

q.q: A port with port security set to maximum 2 MACs and violation mode shutdown went err-disabled after someone plugged in a small hub with three devices. After removing the hub, how is the port restored?
o: Remove the cause, then shut and no shut the port
Right. An err-disabled port stays down until an admin resets it (shutdown, then no shutdown) or an errdisable recovery timer does.
Reboot the PC so it requests a new DHCP lease on that port
The PC isn't what keeps the port disabled.
Raise the PoE budget
PoE has nothing to do with err-disable from port security.
Clear the ARP cache on the gateway
ARP doesn't control the port's state.

q.q: A link's interface counters keep climbing for CRC errors, but there are no collisions and both sides show 1000/full. What is the most likely cause?
o: A spanning tree topology change flushing the MAC address table
STP changes cause brief flooding, not corrupted frames.
A duplex mismatch
Both sides match at full duplex, so it isn't a duplex problem.
A wrong VLAN on the port
A VLAN problem stops traffic. It doesn't corrupt frames.
Physical layer damage: cable, termination or interference
Right. CRC errors with matching duplex point to frames damaged on the wire.

q.q: During a large event, newly arriving guests get 169.254.x.x addresses, while guests who arrived earlier are fine. The DHCP server is up and reachable. What is most likely wrong?
o: A rogue DHCP server is handing out addresses from another subnet
A rogue server would give a wrong subnet, not APIPA.
The wireless channel is overloaded
Interference slows clients, but new ones would still get DHCP addresses.
The DNS server is down
DNS failure doesn't stop clients from getting an IP.
Scope exhaustion: grow the pool or shorten the leases
Right. Every address is leased out, so new clients get no offer and fall back to APIPA.

q.q: Some users on a floor get 192.168.0.x addresses with a gateway of 192.168.0.1, while everyone else gets the normal 10.20.10.x. Users with the 192.168 addresses have no network access. What is the likely cause, and what prevents it?
o: A duplex mismatch. Hard-code the ports.
Duplex doesn't change addressing.
A rogue DHCP server; DHCP snooping prevents it
Right. Often it's a home router someone plugged in. Clients take whichever offer arrives first. Snooping only trusts DHCP server ports you choose.
Scope exhaustion on the real server; shorten the lease time
Exhaustion gives APIPA, not a different private subnet.
A DNS cache problem. Flush DNS.
DNS doesn't assign IP addresses.

q.q: Users can open https://203.0.113.20 but not https://portal.example.mil, and ping 8.8.8.8 works. What should the technician check first?
o: The DHCP scope
Clients already have working IP settings.
The default gateway and the route to the internet
Internet IPs are reachable, so the gateway works.
The cabling
The physical path works, since IP traffic flows.
Name resolution (DNS), with nslookup or dig
Right. Reaching sites by IP but not by name points straight to DNS: check the clients' DNS server settings and the record.

q.q: A host at 10.20.10.57/24 can ping devices in its own subnet but nothing beyond it. ipconfig shows its default gateway as 10.20.11.1. What is the problem?
o: The subnet mask should be /16 so the gateway fits
Changing the mask on one host to make it work creates a mismatch with the rest of the network.
The default gateway is outside the host's subnet
Right. A gateway has to be on the local subnet (10.20.10.0/24). 10.20.11.1 is outside it.
DNS is misconfigured
Pinging by IP fails too, so DNS isn't the issue.
The switch port is in the wrong VLAN
Local pings work, so the host is in the right VLAN.

q.q: A new user's desk port gives him an address from the printer subnet, and he can't reach staff resources. Other users on the same switch are fine. What is the most likely cause?
o: A rogue DHCP server
A rogue server would usually hand out an unexpected subnet to many users, not one.
An expired DHCP lease on his laptop
An expired lease would renew in the same subnet.
A duplex mismatch
Duplex doesn't affect which subnet he gets.
His port is in the wrong VLAN
Right. DHCP hands out addresses from the scope for the port's VLAN, so the wrong VLAN gives the wrong subnet.

q.q: A traceroute to a remote server shows the same two router hops repeating until it ends with "TTL expired in transit." What is the cause?
o: A duplex mismatch
Duplex problems cause errors, not repeating hops.
DNS failure
Traceroute already reached routers by IP, so DNS isn't involved.
A routing loop between those two routers
Right. Each router points to the other for the destination, so packets bounce until the TTL runs out.
The destination server is offline
An offline server would stop the trace at the last hop, not bounce between two routers.

q.q: Over a new site-to-site VPN, pings and small web pages work, but large file transfers and some HTTPS sites hang. A firewall in the path blocks all ICMP. What is the likely cause?
o: Path MTU discovery is broken because ICMP is blocked

Right. Large packets are dropped and the "fragmentation needed" messages never arrive. VPN overhead lowers the usable MTU. Without ICMP feedback, senders keep sending packets that are too big. Clamping MSS or allowing ICMP fixes it.
A DNS server problem
DNS works, since some sites and small pages load.
A DHCP scope that's full
Hosts already have addresses.
Spanning tree reconverging every time a large frame crosses the VPN
STP events cause short outages for all traffic, not just large packets.

q.q: WAN monitoring shows 40 ms latency, 0.1% loss and jitter that swings between 5 and 90 ms. Voice calls sound robotic. Which metric best explains it?
o: Bandwidth
Nothing points to a saturated link. The problem is uneven delay.
Latency
40 ms one-way is well within the range voice handles.
Jitter
Right. Voice needs packets to arrive at an even pace. Big swings in delay overflow the jitter buffer and break up the audio.
Packet loss
0.1% is low enough that voice codecs can usually cover it.

q.q: In a full lecture hall, clients show a strong signal (-55 dBm), but throughput is very poor and retries are high. What is the most likely cause?
o: The DHCP lease time is too short
Lease time doesn't affect throughput.
Contention: a busy channel with co-channel interference
Right. Strong signal doesn't mean capacity. Too many clients and APs on the same channels cause contention and retries that kill throughput.
A wrong VLAN on the AP uplink sending traffic to the guest network
A wrong VLAN would break connectivity, not slow it.
Weak signal at the clients
-55 dBm is a strong signal.

q.q: One TCP file transfer over a 1 Gbps link with 80 ms round-trip time reaches only about 50 Mbps, with no packet loss. What limits it?
o: A duplex mismatch
Duplex mismatches cause errors and collisions, and there's no loss here.
Too little bandwidth on the link for a single file transfer
The link is 1 Gbps, but a single flow can't fill it.
DNS lookups during the transfer
DNS happens once before the transfer starts.
The TCP window size (bandwidth-delay product)
Right. The sender has to wait for ACKs before sending more, so throughput is capped at window ÷ RTT. Filling 1 Gbps at 80 ms needs about a 10 MB window.

q.q: A laptop stays connected to an AP down the hall at -78 dBm even though there's an AP in the same room. Its throughput is poor. What is happening?
o: A sticky client that won't roam to the closer AP
Right. Clients decide when to roam. Some hold on to a weak AP too long. Band steering, roaming assistance, or tuning minimum RSSI and AP power can help.
The laptop has an APIPA address
It's connected and passing traffic, just slowly.
A duplex mismatch on the uplink of the AP down the hall
That would hurt every client on that AP, not just one roaming problem.
The room's AP is in the wrong VLAN
The client never associated with that AP, so its VLAN doesn't matter here.

q.q: A branch's internet link shows 100% outbound use and rising output queue drops during business hours. Users complain about everything being slow. What is the root cause?
o: Congestion: demand exceeds the link's capacity
Right. Output drops at full use mean the link can't keep up. The fix is QoS, shaping, or more bandwidth.
The branch switch's MAC table is full
That causes flooding on the LAN, not WAN queue drops.
DNS is slow
DNS doesn't fill an outbound link.
A routing loop
A loop shows up as TTL expiry and repeating hops, not steady full use with queue drops.

q.q: Which Windows command traces the path to a host and then measures packet loss at each hop over a period of time?
o: netstat
netstat shows local connections and listening ports.
nslookup
nslookup queries DNS.
pathping
Right. pathping runs a trace, then sends probes to each hop for a while to report loss per router.
tracert
tracert lists the hops and their times, but it doesn't measure loss over time.

q.q: On a Linux server, which command shows which process is listening on TCP 443?
o: ss -tlnp
Right. ss with -t (TCP), -l (listening), -n (numeric) and -p (process) lists listening sockets with the owning process.
ip route show
That shows the routing table.
arp -a
arp shows IP-to-MAC mappings.
dig +short 443
dig queries DNS. It doesn't look at local sockets.

q.q: A technician must query the unit's own DNS resolver at 10.20.30.53 for the mail server records of example.mil. Which command does this?
o: ping -a tries to resolve the IP to a name. It doesn't query MX records.
dig @10.20.30.53 example.mil MX
Right. The @ sets which server to ask, and MX asks for mail exchanger records.
nslookup 10.20.30.53
That does a reverse lookup of the resolver's own IP.
-x does a reverse (PTR) lookup of that IP.

q.q: On a network the team is authorized to assess, they need to find unknown devices on a subnet and see which ports each one has open. Which tool fits?
o: tracert
tracert maps the route to one host.
nmap
Right. nmap discovers live hosts and scans their ports. Only run it on networks you're authorized to scan.
A cable tester
A cable tester checks the wiring of one cable.
iperf
iperf measures throughput between two endpoints you control.

q.q: A capture on a client shows repeated SYN packets to 10.20.30.5 on TCP 445 with no reply of any kind. The server is up and answers ping. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The client has the wrong default gateway
The server answers ping, so routing works.
The SMB service is stopped, so the port is closed
A closed port sends back a TCP RST, and the capture shows no reply at all.
A firewall (network or host) is silently dropping TCP 445
Right. A closed port answers with RST. Silence while the host answers ping means a filter is dropping the traffic.
DNS is resolving the wrong name
The capture shows the right IP being used.

q.q: Which tool measures the maximum TCP or UDP throughput between two hosts that the team controls on the network?
o: A Wi-Fi analyzer
A Wi-Fi analyzer shows RF details: channels, signal and noise.
nslookup
nslookup queries DNS.
pathping
pathping reports loss and latency per hop, not maximum throughput.
iperf
Right. iperf runs a client and a server and pushes test traffic between them to measure throughput.

q.q: A wall jack in an old office has no label. Which tool finds which patch panel port it connects to?
o: An OTDR
An OTDR is for fiber.
A loopback adapter
A loopback plug tests a port's own transmit and receive.
A tone generator and probe
Right. The generator puts a tone on the cable at the jack, and the probe finds that tone at the patch panel.
A spectrum analyzer
A spectrum analyzer measures RF, not cable paths.

q.q: A tech needs to know which switch and port an IP phone is plugged into, and the phone and switch support it. Which protocol shows this from the switch side?
o: LLDP (or CDP on Cisco gear)
Right. LLDP neighbor tables list each connected device and the local port it's on.
SMTP
SMTP sends mail.
ARP
ARP maps IP to MAC. It doesn't tell you the port.
NTP
NTP syncs clocks.

q.title: Name the service behind each firewall log line
q.scenario: Five lines from a boat station's firewall log. Pick the service each line shows. Each answer is used once, and two options are distractors.

items.why: A client with no address yet (0.0.0.0) broadcasting from port 68 to server port 67 is a DHCP Discover.
UDP 123 on both ends is NTP time sync.
A device sending to the manager's UDP 162 is an SNMP trap or inform.
UDP 514 toward a collector is traditional syslog.

q.title: Configure the access switch ports
q.scenario: Access switch SW-A1 serves an office. Staff are in VLAN 10, guests in VLAN 20 and switch management in VLAN 99. Set up each port so it meets the requirement.

rows.why: One untagged VLAN for the PC. It's an edge port, so it should forward right away and shut down if a switch is plugged in.

rows.req: Gi1/0/24 connects a ceiling AP with a staff SSID and a guest SSID.
rows.why: Two SSIDs map to two VLANs, so the AP needs a trunk. An AP is an edge device and should never send BPDUs.

rows.req: Gi1/0/48 is the uplink to the distribution switch.
rows.why: The uplink carries every VLAN, including management. BPDU guard here would err-disable the uplink, because STP needs BPDUs between switches.
Unused ports go in a dead VLAN and get shut down, so plugging in gives no access.

q.title: Pick a recovery strategy for each system
q.scenario: A sector is planning disaster recovery. Choose the recovery site and data protection that meet each system's targets at the lowest reasonable cost.

rows.req: Search-and-rescue dispatch: RTO 15 minutes, RPO near zero.
rows.why: Only a hot site with live data copies can take over in minutes with almost no data loss.

rows.req: Personnel portal: RTO 2 days, RPO 24 hours.
rows.why: Ready hardware plus last night's backup meets 2 days and 24 hours without paying for a hot site.

rows.req: Archive file share, changed weekly: RTO 3 weeks, RPO 7 days.
rows.why: With weeks to recover and a week of acceptable loss, the cheapest option meets the targets.

q.title: Pick the right tool for each job
q.scenario: A technician has five jobs this week. Pick the best tool for each. Each answer is used once, and two options are distractors.

items.text: An unlabeled wall jack in Room 12 must be traced to its patch panel port.
items.why: Put a tone on the jack and find it with the probe at the panel.

items.text: A 4 km fiber between two buildings has gone dark. Find how far away the break is.
items.why: An OTDR measures reflections in fiber to find the distance to a break.

items.text: Confirm newly terminated Cat 6a runs have every pin landed correctly before handover.
items.why: A wire map checks continuity and pinout on every conductor.

items.text: Wi-Fi in the hangar is slow. See which channels nearby networks use and the signal levels.
items.why: A Wi-Fi analyzer lists SSIDs, channels and signal strength.

items.text: Measure the real maximum throughput between a server and a branch laptop across the WAN.
items.why: iperf pushes test traffic between two endpoints to measure throughput.
